inflame

/in-FLAYM/ - the stress falls on FLAYM · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Inflame means to stir feelings, tensions, or a conflict into something hotter and more intense.

One mistranslated headline inflamed a border dispute that diplomats had spent the whole summer cooling.

Example

The consultant's slide — half the district labeled 'underused' — inflamed a zoning meeting that had been drowsy for an hour; by the next slide, three residents were on their feet shouting.

Inflame takes feeling that already exists and makes it blaze: irritation becomes fury, a simmering dispute boils over. The prefix is another disguise — this in- means 'into,' not 'not.' The word is built on Latin flamma, 'flame': to inflame is to drive something into flame. That is also why inflammable means burnable, exactly like flammable — nothing in it was ever negated, and warning labels switched to flammable to end the guessing.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

aggravate: To aggravate is to make an existing problem worse — any problem, with no heat required: a delay, a debt, a bad knee. Inflame is aggravation with fire in it: what worsens is feeling, and it worsens by blazing up.

kindle: To kindle is to start a small feeling gently growing — kindle an interest, a hope, a first spark of curiosity. Kindle begins; inflame takes what already burns and drives it into full flame.

enrage: To enrage is to make one person furious — the finished state of a single temper. Inflame heats a whole situation — crowds, disputes, passions — rather than tipping one person over the edge.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

soothe: to calm feeling down and cool it

defuse: to drain the danger out of a tense situation

Where it sits · how hot the stirred feeling burns

provoke → inflame → incense

provoke vs. inflame: To provoke is merely to poke a reaction awake — weaker than inflame, which takes feeling already there and drives it into open flame.

incense vs. inflame: Incense goes further than inflame: an inflamed crowd is heated and loud but can still be argued with, while an incensed one is past reasoning altogether.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-: in, into (Latin) — here 'into flame,' not 'not'

Root — -flame: flame, fire (Latin flamma)

Put it together: Another disguise: the in- of inflame pushes into flame — it intensifies, and negates nothing. Latin flamma gave English its whole fire family, and this word's most famous relative proves the point about the prefix: inflammable means burnable, the same as flammable, because its in- also means 'into.' So many readers guessed wrong that safety labels abandoned the word. When feelings are inflamed, the metaphor is exact — something already warm has been pushed into open fire.

Use the root in a new word: flamboyant: The magician swept onstage in a flamboyant scarlet cape that upstaged the trick itself.

Root Check

Word Choice

charged / negative

Inflame nearly always makes things worse: tensions, rivalries, tempers — and, in medicine, tissue. Aggravate worsens without heat; kindle starts a feeling small; enrage finishes one person's temper. Passion is the exception — a speech can inflame love or ambition — but even there the word promises heat past the point of comfort.
